q: what happens to the human body during deep sea diving
effects of deep sea diving on the human body
what happens to the body when diving deep
scuba diving effects on human body
pressure effects on body during diving
a: Deep sea diving subjects the human body to several significant physiological effects due to increased water pressure. As you descend, water pressure increases by approximately one atmosphere (14.7 psi) every 10 meters (33 feet). The pressure compresses air spaces in the body, including the lungs, sinuses, and middle ear, requiring equalization techniques like the Valsalva maneuver to avoid pain and injury. Nitrogen narcosis, also known as rapture of the deep, occurs when nitrogen dissolves into the bloodstream under pressure, producing an intoxicating effect similar to alcohol or nitrous oxide, typically noticeable below 30 meters (100 feet). This can impair judgment and coordination. Decompression sickness (the bends) occurs when a diver ascends too quickly, causing nitrogen bubbles to form in the blood and tissues, leading to joint pain, paralysis, or death. Divers must follow decompression schedules and safety stops. Oxygen toxicity can occur when breathing high partial pressures of oxygen at depth, potentially causing seizures. The cold water causes hypothermia risk, and increased air density makes breathing harder at depth. Professional divers use specialized gas mixtures like trimix (helium, nitrogen, oxygen) to mitigate these effects. The body also experiences increased blood shift (blood moves from limbs to chest cavity) and increased urination due to immersion diuresis. Despite these risks, with proper training, equipment, and adherence to safety protocols, deep sea diving can be performed safely.
